title: Schedule Jobs With a Cooldown
statement:
A single worker runs jobs, one job per time slot. Each job is a capital letter, and jobs with the same letter are of the same kind. After running a job of some kind, the worker must let at least n slots pass before running that kind again. In those slots it can run other kinds or sit idle.

The jobs in tasks can be run in any order. Return the minimum number of time slots needed to finish all of them, idle slots included.

examples.why: X Y _ X _ _ X. The X jobs need two slots between each pair, and a single Y can fill only one gap. Counting just the jobs would give 4.
P Q R P Q S. There are enough different jobs to fill every gap, so no slot is idle and the answer is the number of jobs.
M N _ _ M N. M and N are tied for the most copies, so the last round holds both of them; counting only one would give 5.

constraints: tasks[i] is an uppercase English letter
hints: The order of the jobs in the input does not matter, only how many of each kind there are. Which kind is most likely to force idle slots?
Greedy: in each slot, among the kinds that are off cooldown, run the one with the most jobs left. A max-heap of remaining counts plus a queue of kinds waiting out their cooldown simulates this.

Or count directly. Let m be the largest count and c the number of kinds with that count. The busiest kind forces m − 1 full blocks of n + 1 slots, then a last block of c slots. The answer is the larger of that and the number of jobs.

explain.intuition:
Only the counts matter. Picture the slots as a timeline. The greedy rule is: in each slot, run the available kind with the most jobs left. Running a kind with few jobs early wastes nothing, but leaving the biggest kind for later bunches its copies together at the end, where they force idle gaps. A max-heap of remaining counts gives that kind in O(log 26). A kind that just ran goes into a queue with the slot at which its cooldown ends, and returns to the heap at that slot. When the heap is empty but the queue is not, the worker idles; jump straight to the next ready slot instead of stepping through idle slots one by one.

The counting formula explains the result. Lay the most frequent kind out as m copies with gaps: that makes m − 1 blocks of n + 1 slots, followed by a last block holding one copy of each of the c kinds tied at m. Every other job fits into the gaps. If there are more jobs than gaps, there is no idle time at all and the answer is just the number of jobs. So the answer is max(tasks.length, (m − 1)(n + 1) + c).
steps: Count the jobs of each kind and push the counts into a max-heap.
Advance time one slot. If the heap is not empty, pop the largest count, run one job of that kind, and if jobs remain, queue (count − 1, time + n).
If the heap is empty, the worker is idle: jump time to the ready time at the front of the queue.
At the end of the slot, if the queue's front is ready at time, move it back into the heap.
Stop when both are empty; time is the answer. (Or compute max(len, (m − 1)(n + 1) + c) directly.)
pitfalls: Returning (m − 1)(n + 1) + 1 and ignoring ties for the top count. Example 3 then gives 5 instead of 6.
Forgetting the max with the number of jobs. When gaps are all filled, as in example 2, the formula alone is too small (4 instead of 6).

In the simulation, picking any available kind instead of the one with the most jobs left. On [Q, Q, Q, R, R, S] with n = 3, running S and R first leaves the Q copies bunched at the end and takes 11 slots instead of 9.

complexity.time: O(T log 26) = O(T) for the simulation, O(T) for the formula, T = number of jobs

solutions.title: Max-heap simulation with a cooldown queue
solutions.idea: Each slot, run the available kind with the most jobs left. Kinds that just ran wait in a queue until their cooldown ends; idle stretches are skipped in one jump.

solutions.title: Count the blocks
solutions.idea: The most frequent kind sets the frame: (m − 1) blocks of n + 1 slots plus one slot for each kind tied at the top count. If the other jobs overflow the gaps, there is no idle time.

followups: Return an actual schedule, with "idle" in the empty slots, not just its length.
The jobs must now run in the given order. How do you compute the number of slots, and why is no heap needed?
